docs.title: Build your own image from your laptop
docs.text:
The platform's images cover the common frameworks, but sooner or later a project needs one more library, a pinned version, or your own code baked in. You don't need Docker on your laptop for that. cscc-cli build uploads your folder, the platform's build engine builds it, and the image lands in your project's private registry, ready for a config file.

In this post you build the image that the two-GPU training and GPU desktop posts use. By the end you have:

  • cscc-cli installed and signed in on your laptop
  • An image with PyTorch, TensorBoard, Matplotlib and your scripts, in your project's registry
  • The image reference to put in a config file

The commands and output below come from a run on the platform on 2026-10-04.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• VPN access, and the Manager role in a project that has Image Build Permission
  • An API token (Settings)
  • About 15 minutes

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: Part Where it runs What it does cscc-cli Your laptop Packs the folder, uploads it and follows the build log Build engine The platform Runs the Dockerfile; one build at a time for everyone Project registry The platform Keeps the image, visible only to your project

docs.title: Step 1: Install cscc-cli
docs.text:
Sign in to the dashboard and open Settings → Security → Downloads (details). Download the file for your system, then on Linux:

chmod +x cscc-cli-linux-amd64
sudo mv cscc-cli-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/cscc-cli

On macOS use the darwin file; on Windows, see Install. The CLI already trusts the platform's certificate.

Sign in with your token and check who you are:

cscc-cli login --api-url https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw --token cscc_...
cscc-cli whoami

login prints where it saved the token, and whoami prints your username and role.

docs.title: Step 2: Write the Dockerfile
docs.text:
Make a folder with the Dockerfile and the two scripts it copies, train_ddp.py and plot_runs.py:

ddp-trainer/
├── Dockerfile
├── train_ddp.py
└── plot_runs.py

FROM pytorch/pytorch:2.14.1-cuda13.0-cudnn9-runtime

# X11 and Tk so the plots can open in a GPU desktop
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get upgrade -y \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libx11-6 libxext6 libxrender1 libxft2 python3-tk xterm fonts-dejavu-core \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
# The image's Python is system-managed (PEP 668)
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --break-system-packages tensorboard==2.20.0 matplotlib==3.10.7

COPY train_ddp.py plot_runs.py /app/
WORKDIR /app

① apt-get upgrade -y pulls in the base image's security fixes, so the security check that runs before the image's first start is less likely to block it. ② This base image marks its Python as system-managed, so pip needs --break-system-packages. Without it the build stops with externally-managed-environment. ③ Install everything at build time. A running container can't apt-get install.

docs.title: Step 3: Build
docs.text:
From inside the folder:

cscc-cli build --project <project id> --name ddp-trainer --tag v1 .

Submitting upload image build for ddp-trainer...
Build job build-arch-ddp-trainer-b0a6ada9 queued. Tag: v1. Destination: 192.168.110.1:30003/p26000001/ddp-trainer:v1
Waiting for build logs...
Streaming build logs...
#5 [1/5] FROM docker.io/pytorch/pytorch:2.14.1-cuda13.0-cudnn9-runtime@sha256:3c0b174a…
#7 [2/5] RUN apt-get update  && apt-get upgrade -y  && apt-get install -y …
…
#11 pushing manifest for 192.168.110.1:30003/p26000001/ddp-trainer:v1@sha256:c2f80e80… done

docs.title: Step 4: Use the image
docs.text:
The Destination line is the image reference. Put it in a config file's image: field:

image: 192.168.110.1:30003/p26000001/ddp-trainer:v1

Train on two GPUs with a config file deploys exactly this.

docs.title: What you built
docs.text:
An image built on the platform from your laptop, with no local Docker, stored where only your project can pull it. Next time:

  • Change the Dockerfile and build again with a new --tag; keep the old tag for configs that still use it.
  • Pass build-time values with --build-arg KEY=VALUE (details).
  • Run cscc-cli build --follow=false to submit and close the terminal; the dashboard keeps the build history.

docs.title: Train on two GPUs with a config file
docs.text:
A training run that fits in a workspace notebook rarely stays there. Once the script works, you want it to run unattended, on more than one GPU, with its results kept. A config file does that: a few lines of YAML that the platform schedules as a job, with your storage mounted and as many GPUs as your plan allows. In the run below, PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP) on two RTX 5090s trained ResNet-18 1.4 times faster than one GPU, to the same accuracy.

In this post you train ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 with DDP, first on one GPU, then on two. By the end you have:

  • A DDP training script that uses every GPU the job gets
  • A config file you deploy from the dashboard, once per GPU count
  • TensorBoard logs and checkpoints in your storage, and a measured comparison

The commands and output below come from a run on the platform on 2026-10-04.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The Manager role in a project with a queue that allows 2 GPUs
  • The ddp-trainer image from Build your own image from your laptop, or any image with PyTorch
  • About 15 minutes

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: Part Where it runs What it does Config file Project Config tab Describes the job: image, command, CPU, memory, GPUs, storage torchrun The job's container Starts one training process per GPU train_ddp.py Each process Trains its share of every batch; DDP averages the gradients /workspace Your storage CIFAR-10, TensorBoard logs, checkpoints

docs.title: Step 1: Write the training script
docs.text:
The image from the previous post already has this file at /app/train_ddp.py:

"""Train ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 with DistributedDataParallel.

Launch with torchrun; every process drives one GPU. Rank 0 writes
TensorBoard logs and checkpoints under --out.
"""
import argparse
import os
import time

import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torchvision
import torchvision.transforms as T
from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, DistributedSampler
from torch.utils.tensorboard import SummaryWriter


def loaders(data_dir, batch_size, rank):
    norm = T.Normalize((0.4914, 0.4822, 0.4465), (0.2470, 0.2435, 0.2616))
    train_tf = T.Compose([T.RandomCrop(32, padding=4), T.RandomHorizontalFlip(), T.ToTensor(), norm])
    if rank == 0:  # one download, the other ranks wait at the barrier
        torchvision.datasets.CIFAR10(data_dir, train=True, download=True)
        torchvision.datasets.CIFAR10(data_dir, train=False, download=True)
    dist.barrier()
    train = torchvision.datasets.CIFAR10(data_dir, train=True, transform=train_tf)
    test = torchvision.datasets.CIFAR10(data_dir, train=False, transform=T.Compose([T.ToTensor(), norm]))
    sampler = DistributedSampler(train)
    train_dl = DataLoader(train, batch_size, sampler=sampler, num_workers=6, pin_memory=True, persistent_workers=True)
    test_dl = DataLoader(test, 1000, num_workers=2)
    return train_dl, test_dl, sampler


def accuracy(model, test_dl, device):
    model.eval()
    correct = 0
    with torch.no_grad(), torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        for x, y in test_dl:
            correct += (model(x.to(device)).argmax(1) == y.to(device)).sum().item()
    model.train()
    return correct / len(test_dl.dataset)


def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--data", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--out", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--epochs", type=int, default=10)
    p.add_argument("--batch-size", type=int, default=256, help="per GPU")
    args = p.parse_args()

    dist.init_process_group("nccl")
    rank, world = dist.get_rank(), dist.get_world_size()
    device = torch.device("cuda", int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"]))
    torch.cuda.set_device(device)

    train_dl, test_dl, sampler = loaders(args.data, args.batch_size, rank)
    model = torchvision.models.resnet18(num_classes=10).to(device, memory_format=torch.channels_last)
    model = DDP(model, device_ids=[device.index])
    lr = 0.1 * args.batch_size * world / 256  # linear scaling rule
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr, momentum=0.9, weight_decay=5e-4, nesterov=True)
    sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR(opt, lr, epochs=args.epochs, steps_per_epoch=len(train_dl))
    loss_fn = torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    writer = SummaryWriter(os.path.join(args.out, f"gpus{world}")) if rank == 0 else None

    for epoch in range(args.epochs):
        sampler.set_epoch(epoch)
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        start = time.time()
        for x, y in train_dl:
            x = x.to(device, non_blocking=True, memory_format=torch.channels_last)
            y = y.to(device, non_blocking=True)
            with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
                loss = loss_fn(model(x), y)
            opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
            loss.backward()
            opt.step()
            sched.step()
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        seconds = time.time() - start
        if rank == 0:
            acc = accuracy(model.module, test_dl, device)
            imgs = len(train_dl.dataset) / seconds
            writer.add_scalar("train/loss", loss.item(), epoch)
            writer.add_scalar("test/accuracy", acc, epoch)
            writer.add_scalar("throughput/images_per_sec", imgs, epoch)
            print(f"epoch {epoch + 1}/{args.epochs}  loss {loss.item():.3f}  "
                  f"test acc {acc:.3f}  {seconds:.1f}s  {imgs:.0f} img/s", flush=True)
    if rank == 0:
        torch.save(model.module.state_dict(), os.path.join(args.out, f"resnet18-gpus{world}.pt"))
        writer.close()
    dist.destroy_process_group()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

① DistributedSampler hands each process a different slice of the data, so two GPUs see each image once per epoch between them. ② The learning rate grows with the number of GPUs (0.1 × batch × GPUs / 256), because the effective batch grows too. ③ Only rank 0 downloads the data, writes logs and saves the model; the others wait at dist.barrier().

docs.title: Step 2: Write the config file
docs.text:
Open Projects → [your project] → Config, click New File, and paste this as ddp-gpus2.yaml:

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: ddp-resnet18-gpus2
spec:
  backoffLimit: 0
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        platform-go/dra-gpu-model: rtx5090
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: train
          image: 192.168.110.1:30003/p26000001/ddp-trainer:v1
          command: ["torchrun", "--nproc_per_node=2", "/app/train_ddp.py",
                    "--data", "/workspace/cifar10", "--out", "/workspace/ddp-runs",
                    "--epochs", "15"]
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "16"
              memory: 48Gi
              nvidia.com/gpu-dra: "2"
            limits:
              cpu: "16"
              memory: 48Gi
              nvidia.com/gpu-dra: "2"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: storage
              mountPath: /workspace
      volumes:
        - name: storage
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: "{{userVolume}}"

① The platform-go/dra-gpu-model label and the nvidia.com/gpu-dra count are what the Resource Wizard writes when you pick a GPU model and count. The deploy dialog reads the model from the label. ② CPU and memory grow with the GPUs. Each training process runs six data-loading workers, and with eight CPUs for two GPUs the GPUs wait for data. ③ {{userVolume}} mounts your personal storage at /workspace, so the data and results outlive the job.

For the one-GPU run, save a copy as ddp-gpus1.yaml with the name ddp-resnet18-gpus1, --nproc_per_node=1, nvidia.com/gpu-dra: "1", 8 CPUs and 24Gi.

docs.title: Step 3: Deploy
docs.text:
Click Deploy on the file's version row, pick the queue, and confirm. The job appears under Resources → Pods; open its logs to follow the training:

epoch 1/15  loss 1.601  test acc 0.462  2.1s  23773 img/s
epoch 2/15  loss 1.469  test acc 0.506  1.5s  32684 img/s
epoch 3/15  loss 1.008  test acc 0.559  1.5s  33115 img/s
…
epoch 13/15  loss 0.448  test acc 0.803  2.0s  25552 img/s
epoch 14/15  loss 0.411  test acc 0.816  1.6s  30847 img/s
epoch 15/15  loss 0.433  test acc 0.821  1.6s  30897 img/s

Before its first start, an image is scanned for known vulnerabilities; the pod waits in that step for a few minutes the first time and starts at once after that. The first run also downloads CIFAR-10 (170 MB) into /workspace/cifar10.

docs.title: Step 4: Compare one and two GPUs
docs.text:
Deploy ddp-gpus1.yaml the same way. Both runs train for 15 epochs:

GPUs Training time Images per second Test accuracy 1 35.7 s 21,230 82.7% 2 24.9 s 30,530 82.1%
  • Two GPUs are 1.4 times as fast, and reach the same accuracy within run-to-run noise.
  • The speed-up is below 2 because ResNet-18 on 32×32 images finishes a step in milliseconds. Every step still loads and augments images on the CPU and averages gradients between the GPUs, and those costs don't shrink with a second GPU. A larger model or larger images spend more of each step on the GPU and scale closer to 2.

Each run leaves a folder under /workspace/ddp-runs/ (gpus1/, gpus2/) with TensorBoard logs, and a checkpoint such as resnet18-gpus2.pt. Look at training results in a GPU desktop plots them.

docs.title: What you built
docs.text:
A training job you describe once in YAML and deploy on as many GPUs as the queue allows, with every run's logs and checkpoints in your storage. To use it for your own model:

  • Swap the dataset and model in train_ddp.py; keep DistributedSampler, DDP(...) and the rank-0 checks.
  • Change only the GPU count, --nproc_per_node and the CPUs and memory to scale up.
  • Deleting a finished job's instance frees its entry; the files in /workspace stay.

docs.title: Serve a 14B LLM across two GPUs with vLLM
docs.text:
Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct is a capable open model, and in 16-bit precision its weights alone take about 28 GB. That is nearly all of a 32 GB RTX 5090, leaving no room for the KV cache, the memory each conversation needs. Tensor parallelism splits every layer across two GPUs, so each card holds half the weights and the rest goes to the cache. In the run below, vLLM on two RTX 5090s served the model at 2,625 tokens per second across 64 parallel requests. On one card it would not start at all.

In this post you serve the model from a workspace and call it with the OpenAI Python client. By the end you have:

  • The model's weights in group storage, downloaded once and reused by every server you start
  • A vLLM server on two GPUs with an OpenAI-compatible API
  • Measured throughput for one request and for 64 at once, and proof that one GPU is not enough

The commands and output below come from a run on the platform on 2026-10-04.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A project with a queue that allows 2 GPUs, and a group storage volume with about 35 GB free bound to it (Storage)
  • A workspace in that project with the group volume ticked; it needs no GPU of its own
  • About 30 minutes, most of it the one-time download

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: Part Where it runs What it does Workspace The platform Your terminal: downloads the model, starts and calls the server vLLM server Its own job with 2 GPUs Loads half of every layer on each GPU and answers OpenAI API calls models/ Group storage The 29.5 GB of weights, shared by every server and lab member

docs.title: Step 1: Download the model into group storage
docs.text:
Check free space with df -h /home/<your username> /mnt/shared/<volume name>. In this run personal storage had 10 GiB, too small for the model, so it goes to group storage, where your lab can reuse it too. In the workspace terminal:

pip install --user "huggingface_hub[hf_xet]==1.32.0"
export PATH=$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH
hf download Qwen/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct --local-dir /mnt/shared/<volume name>/models/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct

The download is 29.5 GB in eight files. It resumes where it stopped if the workspace restarts, so run the same command again.

docs.title: Step 2: Start the server on two GPUs
docs.text:
Workspaces have a docker command that starts containers next to the workspace (Using docker in the IDE):

docker run -d --keep --name qwen14b --gpus 2 --cpus 8 -m 48g --shm-size 8g \
  -p 8000:8000 \
  -v /mnt/shared/<volume name>/models:/models:ro \
  -e HOME=/tmp \
  vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0 \
  --model /models/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct --served-model-name qwen2.5-14b \
  --tensor-parallel-size 2 --max-model-len 8192

① --keep --gpus 2 gives the container two GPUs of its own, from your project's quota. The workspace has no GPU to share, so the container gets its own. ② -p 8000:8000 publishes the API on 127.0.0.1:8000 inside the workspace. ③ -v …:/models:ro mounts the weights read-only, so a server can never damage the shared copy. ④ -e HOME=/tmp keeps vLLM's compile cache inside the container instead of in a home folder. ⑤ --tensor-parallel-size 2 splits each layer across the two GPUs.

Follow the start-up with docker logs -f qwen14b. The lines that matter:

Model loading took 13.93 GiB memory and 47.540906 seconds
GPU KV cache size: 149,488 tokens, Maximum concurrency for 8,192 tokens per request: 18.25x
init engine (profile, create kv cache, warmup model) took 176.75 s (compilation: 20.35 s)
Application startup complete.

Each GPU holds 13.93 GiB, half the weights, and the rest of its memory holds a 149,488-token cache: room for 18 full-length conversations at once. In this run the server was ready 8 minutes after docker run. Of that, 2 minutes 42 seconds was the image's security check and first pull, which later starts skip.

docs.title: Step 3: Call the model
docs.text:
The server speaks the OpenAI API, so the official client works with only the base URL changed. Save this as bench.py in the workspace:

"""Ask the vLLM server one question, then measure throughput under load.

Usage: python bench.py [concurrent requests]
"""
import asyncio
import sys
import time

from openai import AsyncOpenAI

client = AsyncOpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1", api_key="unused")
MODEL = "qwen2.5-14b"


async def ask(prompt, max_tokens=256):
    r = await client.chat.completions.create(
        model=MODEL, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        max_tokens=max_tokens, temperature=0.7)
    return r.choices[0].message.content, r.usage.completion_tokens


async def main(n):
    start = time.time()
    answer, tokens = await ask("用三句話解釋什麼是 tensor parallelism。")
    print(f"{answer}\n-- {tokens} tokens in {time.time() - start:.2f}s\n")

    prompts = [f"Write a short story about GPU number {i}." for i in range(n)]
    start = time.time()
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(ask(p) for p in prompts))
    seconds = time.time() - start
    total = sum(t for _, t in results)
    print(f"{n} concurrent requests: {total} tokens in {seconds:.1f}s = {total / seconds:,.0f} tokens/s")


asyncio.run(main(int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 64))

pip install --user openai==2.8.1
python bench.py 1
python bench.py 64

Tensor parallelism是一種在深度學習模型訓練中分發計算和數據的方法，它將大型張量（多維數組）分割成更小的部分，並在不同的處理器或設備上並行處理這些部分。這種技術可以加速模型的訓練過程並允許使用更大的模型和數據集。
-- 68 tokens in 1.01s

1 concurrent requests: 256 tokens in 2.9s = 88 tokens/s
…
64 concurrent requests: 16384 tokens in 6.2s = 2,625 tokens/s

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Setup Result 2 GPUs, 1 request 88 tokens/s 2 GPUs, 64 requests at once 2,625 tokens/s 1 GPU Does not start: No available memory for the cache blocks
  • One request at a time uses a fraction of the GPUs. vLLM batches concurrent requests together, so 64 at once produced 30 times the tokens per second.
  • On one GPU, the same command with --gpus 1 and no --tensor-parallel-size loaded 27.57 GiB of weights, then stopped: there was no memory left for the KV cache. Two GPUs are what make this model servable on these cards at all.

docs.title: Step 4: Stop the server
docs.text:
A --keep container keeps its GPUs even after the workspace stops, and counts toward your project's job limits and GPU hours. Remove it when you're done:

docker rm -f qwen14b

The weights stay in group storage for next time; the next start skips the download.

  • Try a larger model with --gpus 4 --tensor-parallel-size 4 if your plan allows four GPUs.
  • Serve a quantized build (for example an AWQ variant) when one GPU is all you can get.
  • Keep the vLLM version pinned; a new tag waits for its security check the first time it starts.

docs.title: Score a dataset on GPUs with Ray Data
docs.text:
Batch inference is the part of a project nobody budgets for: the model is trained, and now ten million rows need a score. In a workspace that is one GPU working through the whole file. With Ray Data, each GPU worker loads the model once and takes its share of the rows. In the run below, two RTX 5090s scored 10 million rows in 184 seconds, 1.99 times faster than one.

In this post you score a Parquet dataset with a multilayer perceptron on one GPU, then on two. By the end you have:

  • A Ray Data script that loads the model once per GPU and streams batches through it
  • Inputs, model and scores in your storage, where the next step of your pipeline can read them
  • A measured comparison of one and two GPUs

The commands and output below come from a run on the platform on 2026-10-04.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Your laptop set up for Ray jobs, as in step 1 of Sweep hyperparameters across GPUs with Ray, with "X-CSCC-GPUs":"2"
  • About 3 GB free in your storage
  • About 15 minutes

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text:
Part Where it runs What it does batch_score.py Ray session Creates the data and model the first time, then times one and two GPUs Scorer One per GPU worker Loads the weights onto its GPU once and scores each batch with CuPy ray-batch/ Your storage input/ (10 million rows, 64 features), mlp-4096.npz, and one scores-* folder per run

The model is an MLP with three hidden layers of 4,096 units and random weights. Swap in your own model as shown under What you built; the rest stays the same.

docs.title: Step 1: Write the script
docs.text:
Save this as batch_score.py in an empty folder:

"""Score a Parquet dataset on GPU workers with Ray Data.

Each GPU worker loads the model once, then scores batches with CuPy.
Inputs and outputs live in your storage.
"""
import argparse
import os
import shutil
import time

import numpy as np
import ray

FEATURES = 64


def make_rows(batch):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(int(batch["id"][0]))
    batch["features"] = rng.standard_normal((len(batch["id"]), FEATURES), dtype=np.float32)
    return batch


def make_model(path, hidden=4096, layers=3, seed=0):
    """Stand-in for your trained model: an MLP with random weights."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    sizes = [FEATURES] + [hidden] * layers + [1]
    np.savez(path, *(rng.standard_normal((a, b), dtype=np.float32) / np.sqrt(a)
                     for a, b in zip(sizes, sizes[1:])))


class Scorer:
    def __init__(self, model_path):
        import cupy as cp
        self.cp = cp
        weights = np.load(model_path)
        self.layers = [cp.asarray(weights[f"arr_{i}"]) for i in range(len(weights.files))]
        gpu = cp.cuda.runtime.getDeviceProperties(0)["name"].decode()
        self.worker = f"{gpu} on node {ray.get_runtime_context().get_node_id()[:8]}"

    def __call__(self, batch):
        cp = self.cp
        h = cp.asarray(batch["features"])
        for w in self.layers[:-1]:
            h = cp.maximum(h @ w, 0)
        score = 1 / (1 + cp.exp(-(h @ self.layers[-1])[:, 0]))
        return {"id": batch["id"], "score": cp.asnumpy(score), "worker": np.full(len(score), self.worker)}


def score(inputs, outputs, model, gpus):
    shutil.rmtree(outputs, ignore_errors=True)
    start = time.time()
    ray.data.read_parquet(inputs).map_batches(
        Scorer, fn_constructor_kwargs={"model_path": model},
        compute=ray.data.ActorPoolStrategy(size=gpus), num_gpus=1, batch_size=50_000,
    ).write_parquet(outputs)
    return time.time() - start


def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument("--data", required=True, help="folder in your storage")
    p.add_argument("--rows", type=int, default=10_000_000)
    p.add_argument("--max-gpus", type=int, default=2)
    args = p.parse_args()
    inputs, model = os.path.join(args.data, "input"), os.path.join(args.data, "mlp-4096.npz")
    if not os.path.exists(inputs):
        ray.data.range(args.rows, override_num_blocks=40).map_batches(make_rows).write_parquet(inputs)
    if not os.path.exists(model):
        make_model(model)

    # Warm-up: start every GPU worker and compile the kernels before timing.
    score(inputs, os.path.join(args.data, "warmup"), model, args.max_gpus)

    for gpus in range(1, args.max_gpus + 1):
        outputs = os.path.join(args.data, f"scores-{gpus}gpu")
        seconds = score(inputs, outputs, model, gpus)
        out = ray.data.read_parquet(outputs)
        rows = out.count()
        print(f"{gpus} GPU: {rows:,} rows in {seconds:.1f} s = {rows / seconds:,.0f} rows/s")
        print(out.groupby("worker").count().to_pandas().to_string(index=False))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

① ActorPoolStrategy(size=gpus) with num_gpus=1 starts one Scorer per GPU. Ray Data hands each one batches as it finishes the last, so a slower GPU never holds up the others. ② The model loads in __init__, once per worker, not once per batch. ③ The first score call is a warm-up. It starts both GPU workers before anything is timed, so the comparison measures scoring, not start-up.

docs.title: Step 2: Submit the job
docs.text:
ray job submit --working-dir . -- python batch_score.py --data /home/<your username>/ray-batch

The first run also writes the 10 million input rows (about 3 GB) to your storage. In this run the whole job, warm-up included, took 12 minutes 35 seconds.

docs.title: Sweep hyperparameters across GPUs with Ray
docs.text:
Trying eight hyperparameter combinations one after another in a workspace takes eight times as long as one. With a Ray job, you send the whole sweep from your laptop and the platform runs one combination per GPU at the same time. In the run below, all eight trials finished in 17 seconds on two RTX 5090s.

In this post you run a learning-rate and L2 sweep on two GPUs. By the end you have:

  • A Ray Tune script that gives each trial its own GPU
  • The sweep running on the platform, sent from your laptop
  • Every trial's results in your storage, and the best setting printed

The commands and output below come from a run on the platform on 2026-10-03.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• VPN access, a project you belong to, and an API token (Settings)
  • Python 3.10 or later on your laptop
  • A queue that allows 2 GPUs in your project
  • About 10 minutes

docs.text: Part Where it runs What it does ray command Your laptop Uploads the folder, sends the job, shows the output Ray session The platform Starts on the first submit, ends after 30 idle minutes or at its maximum lifetime GPU workers The platform One per running trial, up to X-CSCC-GPUs ray-results/ Your storage Each trial's settings and per-epoch metrics

docs.title: Step 1: Set up your laptop
docs.text:
Install Ray, trust the platform's Root certificate (from Settings → Security → Downloads), and say what you need. Submit a job explains each line.

pip install "ray[default]==2.58.0"
export REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE=~/Downloads/cscc-root-ca.pem
export SSL_CERT_FILE=~/Downloads/cscc-root-ca.pem
export RAY_JOB_HEADERS='{"Authorization":"Bearer cscc_xxx","X-CSCC-GPUs":"2","X-CSCC-Queue":"<queue>"}'
export RAY_ADDRESS=https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw/api/v1/projects/<project id>/ray

With RAY_ADDRESS set, ray job commands need no --address. If your plan and queue allow more than one GPU model, also add "X-CSCC-GPU-Model":"<model>" to the headers.

docs.title: Step 2: Write the sweep
docs.text:
The platform's Ray image has NumPy, CuPy, pandas, Ray Tune and Ray Data, but no PyTorch, so the model is a logistic regression in CuPy. Save this as sweep.py in an empty folder:

"""Sweep learning rate and L2 strength for a logistic-regression model on GPU.

Each trial trains on one GPU with CuPy; Ray Tune runs one trial per GPU worker.
"""
import argparse

import cupy as cp
from ray import tune


def make_data(n=200_000, d=512, seed=0):
    rng = cp.random.default_rng(seed)
    w_true = rng.standard_normal(d, dtype=cp.float32)
    x = rng.standard_normal((n, d), dtype=cp.float32)
    y = (x @ w_true + 0.5 * rng.standard_normal(n, dtype=cp.float32) > 0).astype(cp.float32)
    split = int(n * 0.8)
    return x[:split], y[:split], x[split:], y[split:]


def train(config):
    x, y, xv, yv = make_data()
    w = cp.zeros(x.shape[1], dtype=cp.float32)
    for epoch in range(config["epochs"]):
        p = 1 / (1 + cp.exp(-(x @ w)))
        grad = x.T @ (p - y) / len(y) + config["l2"] * w
        w -= config["lr"] * grad
        acc = float(((xv @ w > 0) == (yv > 0.5)).mean())
        tune.report({"val_acc": acc, "epoch": epoch + 1,
                     "gpu": cp.cuda.runtime.getDeviceProperties(0)["name"].decode()})


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--out", required=True, help="results folder in your storage")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    tuner = tune.Tuner(
        tune.with_resources(train, {"gpu": 1}),
        param_space={
            "lr": tune.grid_search([0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 5.0]),
            "l2": tune.grid_search([0.0, 0.01]),
            "epochs": 50,
        },
        tune_config=tune.TuneConfig(metric="val_acc", mode="max"),
        run_config=tune.RunConfig(name="lr-l2-sweep", storage_path=args.out),
    )
    results = tuner.fit()
    df = results.get_dataframe()[["config/lr", "config/l2", "val_acc", "gpu"]]
    print(df.sort_values("val_acc", ascending=False).to_string(index=False))
    print("best:", results.get_best_result().config)

① tune.with_resources(train, {"gpu": 1}): one GPU per trial, so Ray starts one worker per running trial. ② storage_path=args.out: results go to your storage, because the cluster's own disk is gone when it ends.

docs.title: Look at training results in a GPU desktop
docs.text:
Training logs are numbers in a file until you plot them, and the files live on the platform, not on your laptop. A GPU desktop gives you a Linux desktop in the browser with your own image and your storage mounted, so you can open a plotting window right next to the data, with no download and no port forwarding. The platform adds the desktop around your unchanged image, and a slice of a GPU encodes the screen.

In this post you open a desktop that plots the two-GPU training runs side by side. By the end you have:

  • A config file that starts a Linux desktop with your image
  • An interactive Matplotlib window and a terminal, both reading your storage
  • A desktop you can start again whenever you have new runs

The commands and output below come from a run on the platform on 2026-10-04.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The Manager role in a project where an admin has turned on Remote Desktop Permission
  • The ddp-trainer image from Build your own image from your laptop; it has the X11 and Tk libraries a desktop window needs
  • The TensorBoard logs from Train on two GPUs with a config file in /workspace/ddp-runs
  • About 10 minutes

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: Part Where it runs What it does Desktop The platform, next to your container Draws the screen and streams it to your browser Your container 25% of an RTX 5090 Runs xterm and the plotting script /workspace Your storage The logs to plot

docs.title: Step 1: Write the plotting script
docs.text:
The image already has this file at /app/plot_runs.py:

"""Plot every run under a folder of TensorBoard logs in one window.

Usage: python plot_runs.py /workspace/ddp-runs
"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("TkAgg")  # an on-screen window in the desktop
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # noqa: E402
from tensorboard.backend.event_processing.event_accumulator import EventAccumulator  # noqa: E402

TAGS = [("test/accuracy", "Test accuracy"), ("throughput/images_per_sec", "Images per second"),
        ("train/loss", "Training loss")]

root = Path(sys.argv[1])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(TAGS), figsize=(15, 4.5))
for run in sorted(p for p in root.iterdir() if p.is_dir()):
    events = EventAccumulator(str(run))
    events.Reload()
    for ax, (tag, title) in zip(axes, TAGS):
        points = events.Scalars(tag)
        ax.plot([p.step + 1 for p in points], [p.value for p in points], marker="o", label=run.name)
        ax.set_title(title)
        ax.set_xlabel("epoch")
for ax in axes:
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

It reads every run folder under the path you give it and draws test accuracy, images per second and training loss, one line per run.

docs.title: Step 2: Write the config file
docs.text:
Open Projects → [your project] → Config, click New File, and paste this as results-desktop.yaml:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: results-desktop
spec:
  containers:
    - name: desktop
      image: 192.168.110.1:30003/p26000001/ddp-trainer:v1
      command: ["sh", "-c", "until [ -S /tmp/.X11-unix/X0 ]; do sleep 1; done; xterm & python3 /app/plot_runs.py /workspace/ddp-runs & sleep infinity"]
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: "2"
          memory: 4Gi
        limits:
          cpu: "2"
          memory: 4Gi
      volumeMounts:
        - name: storage
          mountPath: /workspace
  volumes:
    - name: storage
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: "{{userVolume}}"

---

apiVersion: platform.nthu.cc/v1alpha1
kind: RemoteDesktopPolicy
spec:
  workloadName: "results-desktop"
  profile: x11-nvidia
  deviceClassName: "rtx5090.gpu.nvidia.com"
  gpuPercentage: 25
  bitrateProfile: economy

① The RemoteDesktopPolicy block is what the Resource Wizard writes when you turn on Remote desktop under the container. It picks the GPU model, a 25% share of one card, and the Economy stream (1600×900, 30 fps). ② The container asks for no GPU of its own; the desktop fields cover it. ③ The command waits for the desktop's display to appear, starts a terminal and the plot, then keeps the container alive. Without sleep infinity, closing the plot window would end the desktop.

docs.text:
Click Deploy on the version row and pick a queue. Open Sidebar → Workspace → GPU Desktops. In this run the row turned Ready 30 seconds after the deploy, with the hardware encoder.

Click Connect. The desktop opens in a new browser window:

The plot window is a normal Matplotlib window: zoom, pan, and save a PNG into /workspace with the toolbar. The xterm behind it is a shell in your image, with your storage at /workspace.

docs.title: Step 4: End the desktop
docs.text: A desktop lasts at most 8 hours and is reclaimed after 30 minutes with nobody watching. To free the GPU share now, delete the instance from the config file. Anything you saved under /workspace stays.

docs.title: What you built
docs.text:
A desktop that opens your own image in the browser, next to your data, on a quarter of a GPU. To use it for other tools:

  • Replace the command with your GUI program; install it in your image at build time, since the desktop can't apt-get install.
  • Pick 50% GPU or more for heavier 3D work, and Default or High motion for a sharper or smoother picture on campus.
  • Mount group storage instead of {{userVolume}} to look at your lab's shared results.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
• GPU desktops: fields, states, lifetime
  • Matplotlib interactive figures

docs.title: User guide
docs.text: How to sign in, start a GPU workspace, manage projects and groups, use storage, and ask the admins for more.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A current browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari)
  • An account from a platform admin
  • VPN access (the platform is on a private network)
  • The acceptable use rules, read once

docs.title: First steps
docs.text:
Start with Getting started.

First-time checklist

  • [ ] Connect to the VPN
  • [ ] Sign in at https://dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw
  • [ ] Look at the Home dashboard
  • [ ] Check your project's GPU quota under Projects
  • [ ] Launch a workspace

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
Start here

  • Getting started: VPN, sign-in, your first workspace
  • Acceptable use: the rules for compute and storage
  • Concepts and roles: how groups, projects, workspaces and storage fit together, and what each role can do
  • Home dashboard: free GPUs, your quota use, running jobs, recent requests

Run on GPUs

  • Workspaces: JupyterLab or VS Code with a GPU
  • GPU desktops: a GPU desktop or Isaac Sim in your browser
  • Projects: GPU/CPU/memory quotas, config files, members
  • Ray jobs: submit a Ray job from your laptop
  • CLI: cscc-cli for sign-in, image builds and API tokens

Files and teams

  • Storage: volumes that keep your files
  • Groups: teams and courses with shared storage

Account and help

  • Requests: ask the admins for more resources, storage, or an image
  • Announcements: maintenance and rule changes
  • Settings: profile, password, API tokens, notifications, language

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Role What it can do User Use resources within the project's quota Manager Manage projects and groups, and open some admin pages Admin Everything

See Concepts and roles for the full permission tables.

docs.title: Announcements
docs.text:
Announcements are admin messages to everyone. They show as dashboard banners and stay on the Announcements page until they expire; a scheduled one stays hidden until its publish time.

Who can use it: everyone who is signed in.

docs.title: Where announcements appear
docs.text:
Location What you see Home Dashboard Pinned or unread announcements at the top of the page. Sidebar → Announcements All current announcements, with All and Unread filters. Modal view The full title, text, priority, publish date, and expiry date. Overview popup Unread announcements pop up one at a time when you open or reload Overview. Pinned ones come first, then Critical, Warning and Info, newest first. Other pages do not pop up. Notification bell The bell in the header counts unread announcements and lists the latest three above your notifications.

Priority is info, warning, or critical. Critical is usually maintenance, a service problem, or something you must act on.

docs.title: Read and acknowledge
docs.text:
1. Open Announcements from the sidebar, or click View all on a dashboard banner.
  2. Select an announcement to open the detail modal.
  3. Select I've read this. Only this marks it as read; opening it does not.

Closing one with ✕, Escape, or a click outside, or hiding a banner, only hides it until you next open Overview.

If saving your read fails, keep the notice open and try again. Read status follows you across tabs and devices. Admins can see who has read a notice and when they first did.

A new announcement updates the bell right away and pops up if you are on Overview. If the live connection drops, the page checks about once a minute and when you return to the window. Dates are in Taipei time.

A pinned announcement can keep showing after you read it, until an admin unpins it or it expires.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
Why did an announcement disappear?

It probably expired, or an admin removed it.

Can I reply to an announcement?

No. To ask about a notice or get help, send a request.

docs.title: Command Line Interface
docs.text:
cscc-cli signs in, builds images, follows build logs, runs docker in the IDE and manages your API tokens.

Who can use it: everyone who is signed in.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Workspaces already have cscc-cli. On your own computer, download it from Settings → Security → Downloads in the dashboard, then:

chmod +x cscc-cli-linux-amd64
sudo mv cscc-cli-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/cscc-cli

On macOS, use the darwin file; if macOS blocks it the first time, run xattr -d com.apple.quarantine /usr/local/bin/cscc-cli. On Windows, put cscc-cli-windows-amd64.exe in a folder on your Path and rename it cscc-cli.exe.

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
On a new machine, set the API URL with --api-url or CSCC_API_URL (a trailing /api/v1 is fine). Precedence: --api-url, then CSCC_API_URL, then the saved config.

cscc-cli login --api-url https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw --username alice

The CLI asks for your password, with no CAPTCHA, and saves a cscc_... API token in a config file only you can read. A token shows only once, when created.

To name the token:

cscc-cli login --api-url https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw --username alice --name workstation

A token name is up to 100 characters; the default is cscc-cli.

docs.title: Import a dashboard-created token
docs.text:
Create a token under Settings → API Key & CLI and import it:

cscc-cli login --api-url https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw --token cscc_...

The CLI checks the token before saving it. Use this to avoid typing your password in a terminal.

docs.title: Stateless token override
docs.text:
For scripts, set CSCC_API_TOKEN instead of saving a config file:

CSCC_API_URL=https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw CSCC_API_TOKEN=cscc_... cscc-cli whoami

CSCC_DEV_TOKEN is deprecated; use CSCC_API_TOKEN.

docs.title: TLS / Internal CA
docs.text:
The CLI from Downloads already trusts the platform's certificate; if it changes, download the latest one. Use these variables only for custom builds and TLS troubleshooting:

Env Description CSCC_API_URL API base URL, e.g. https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw/api/v1 CSCC_API_TOKEN Optional stateless cscc_... token override CSCC_API_CA_CERT_PATH One or multiple PEM files separated by , or ; CSCC_API_TLS_SERVER_NAME Optional TLS SNI name (fallback to config if not set) SSL_CERT_FILE Path to a PEM file containing the internal root CA REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE Alternative env path for a PEM bundle containing the internal root CA

Example:

CSCC_API_CA_CERT_PATH=/Users/me/platform-internal-root-ca.pem \
  cscc-cli login --api-url https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw --username alice

docs.title: Check Identity
docs.text:
cscc-cli whoami

Checks your saved token and prints your user and role. Role changes apply right away.

docs.title: Build Images
docs.text:
Upload mode is the default. Give it a folder, a .tar.gz or a .zip:

cscc-cli build --project <project-id> --name trainer --tag v1.0.1 .
cscc-cli build --project <project-id> --name trainer ./context.tar.gz

The CLI packs a folder into a .tar.gz. The Dockerfile must be at the top level.

Dockerfile-only mode, like pasting a Dockerfile in the dashboard:

cscc-cli build --source dockerfile \
  --project <project-id> \
  --name trainer \
  --tag v1.0.1 \
  --dockerfile ./Dockerfile

cat Dockerfile | cscc-cli build --source dockerfile \
  --project <project-id> \
  --name trainer \
  --dockerfile -

Options:

Option Description --project Project ID the image build belongs to --name Short image name, for example trainer-api --tag Optional image tag. Omit it to use the platform default --source upload or dockerfile --dockerfile Dockerfile path, or - for stdin, when --source dockerfile --build-arg Dockerfile ARG override as KEY=VALUE; repeatable --follow=false Submit the build without streaming logs

docs.title: Build arguments
docs.text:
Pass Dockerfile ARG values with --build-arg KEY=VALUE (repeatable) in upload and dockerfile builds. A KEY starts with a letter or underscore and has only letters, digits and underscores.

cscc-cli build --project <project-id> --name trainer --tag v1 \
  --build-arg HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx \
  --build-arg MAX_JOBS=4 \
  .

Use it to keep secrets out of the committed Dockerfile (ARG HF_TOKEN), or to limit compile parallelism (MAX_JOBS, FLASH_ATTN_MAX_JOBS, …) so a heavy build fits the shared build engine.

Anyone who can inspect the build can see build args, so don't put anything very sensitive in them, and replace any token you pass this way once the build is done.

docs.title: Shared build queue
docs.text:
One shared build engine runs one build at a time, with fixed CPU, memory and scratch space. It shuts down when idle, so the first build after that waits about a minute.

--follow=true (the default) streams logs until the build reports completed, failed or deleted.

The project must have Image Build Permission on, and your project role must allow builds.

docs.title: Using docker in the IDE
docs.text: Jupyter and VS Code workspaces have a docker command that works like Docker. Each container starts next to the workspace, in the same project, and counts toward the project's quota; nothing runs inside the workspace.

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text: A workspace started after the platform update needs no sign-in. An older workspace needs cscc-cli login, runs every container as a separate job and prints restart your workspace for full docker support; delete it and start a new one (storage is kept).

docs.title: Run a container
docs.text:
docker run --rm alpine echo hello
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:8000 python:3.12 python -m http.server 8000
curl localhost:8080
docker ps
docker logs -f web
docker stop web

Output streams to your terminal and the command exits with the container's exit code.

Without -t, Ctrl-C acts as Docker's signal proxy. The first press sends SIGINT to the main process (the image needs /bin/sh; otherwise the container is stopped). The second press stops the container (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10 seconds). The third press detaches and leaves it stopping. With -t, Ctrl-C goes to the program in the container.

docker run -d shows Waiting: … until the container runs, then prints its ID. If it can't start, it prints the reason, removes the container and exits 125. Ctrl-C stops the waiting, not the start.

docs.title: What works like Docker
docs.text:
• Only the paths you mount are visible inside the container. Mount a folder with -v SRC:DST[:ro] or --mount type=bind,source=SRC,target=DST. Write a relative SRC as ./data or ../data; a bare data is a named volume, which doesn't exist. -v creates a missing SRC; --mount fails.
  • SRC must be under your home folder or a group storage folder. Read-only storage stays read-only inside the container.
  • The image's own WORKDIR, ENTRYPOINT and CMD apply. Your command after the image name replaces CMD, and --entrypoint replaces the entrypoint.
  • Without -u, a container runs as the image's numeric USER (for example USER 101). With no USER, or only a name such as USER app, it runs as user 1000, your workspace's user, so files in your storage stay editable. -u 0 and USER 0 run as root only when the project (and, for a group's project, the group) allows root containers; otherwise user 1000.
  • A container gets 1 CPU and 4 GiB of memory unless you set --cpus and -m. --shm-size sets the size of /dev/shm.
  • -e KEY=VALUE, -e KEY (copies your value), --env-file, -w, --rm and -d work as in Docker.
  • --name takes 2 to 63 letters, digits, _, . and -, and must start and end with a letter or digit.
  • --entrypoint "" clears the image's entrypoint. Then give the command after the image name.

docs.title: GPUs
docs.text:
Command What you get docker run --gpus all … or --gpus N The container shares your workspace's GPU and adds no GPU quota or GPU hours. N can't be more than the workspace has. --gpus device=0,1 picks cards by index, not by UUID. docker run --keep --gpus N … N new GPUs for the container, from your project's quota and plan, in the same queue as the workspace. They count toward GPU hours. With --keep, --gpus takes a number only.

A workspace without a GPU refuses --gpus all and --gpus N with this workspace has no GPU to share; use --keep --gpus N to allocate one for the container. A container sharing the workspace's GPU also shares its memory.

docs.title: Containers and the workspace
docs.text:
A container ends with its workspace (delete, idle limit, runtime limit or pause) and doesn't come back when the workspace resumes. A running container counts as activity, so the workspace isn't stopped as idle.

--keep detaches a container: it keeps running after the workspace stops, counts as an ordinary job against your project's job limits, and can't share the workspace's GPU. Stop it with docker stop.

A finished container stays in docker ps -a, with its logs, for 24 hours, and its name stays taken. docker ps -a lists containers from all your workspaces in this project.

A container stopped by its workspace shows Exited (137), its logs are gone, and docker logs answers can not get logs from container which is dead or marked for removal.

--rm removes the container once docker run has shown its exit code; a -d container is removed about a minute after it exits. Otherwise docker rm or docker container prune removes finished containers earlier.

docs.title: Stop, kill and remove
docs.text:
• docker stop sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10 seconds. -t is accepted, but the 10 seconds are fixed. The container stays in docker ps -a as Exited (143) or Exited (137), and its logs remain.
  • docker kill also sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10 seconds, so the exit code can be 143 or 0 rather than 137. The container stays in docker ps -a. docker kill -s HUP (or USR1, INT, …) reaches the main process through a shell, so the image needs /bin/sh, and the program ignores the signal unless it handles it. Failed delivery prints could not deliver SIGHUP: ….
  • docker rm removes a finished container. docker rm -f kills a running one first.

docs.title: Ports and the browser
docs.text:
-p 8080:8000 forwards port 8080 of the workspace to port 8000 of the container. In the workspace terminal:

curl localhost:8080

The port is open on localhost only, TCP only. -p 8000 alone picks a free port; docker port web shows it. A port already in use fails with port is already allocated. Forwarding survives Ctrl-C and ends when the container exits.

To open the app in your browser, start from the workspace address (click Open):

https://<platform host>/api/v1/ide/proxy/<workspace name>/

Then add proxy/8080/:

https://<platform host>/api/v1/ide/proxy/<workspace name>/proxy/8080/

This works in JupyterLab and VS Code workspaces. Keep the trailing slash. The platform strips proxy/8080 before the request reaches your app, so absolute links such as /static/app.js fail; use relative links or set the app's base path to the full address.

docs.title: Interactive containers, exec and copy
docs.text:
docker run -it ubuntu bash
docker exec -it web sh
docker attach web
docker cp ./results.csv web:/tmp/
docker cp web:/var/log/app.log .
  • -it opens a terminal in the container. Press Ctrl-P, then Ctrl-Q, to leave a terminal session without stopping the container.
  • docker exec takes -i, -t, -d, -e and -w, but not -u. -e values can appear in the platform's API logs; pass secrets through a file in your storage.
  • docker attach joins the container's main process.
  • docker cp goes through tar, so the image needs tar. Links are copied as links, never followed; a copy refuses to write through a link or onto one, and refuses to replace a folder with a file or the reverse.
  • An exec or attach session ends after 24 hours.

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
docker build -t myimg .
docker run myimg
docker images

docker build uploads the folder, builds it on the platform and stores the image in your project. The FROM image can come from any registry; the platform scans it automatically. -f takes a Dockerfile from any path, --build-arg KEY=VALUE and .dockerignore work as in Docker, and the Dockerfile is always sent. A bare name such as myimg or myimg:v2 (no registry, no /) then runs your build instead of a public image of the same name. docker images lists your project's builds.

Like cscc-cli build, building needs the Project Manager role or above and Image Build Permission on the project.

Every image is security-checked before its container starts; docker run shows Waiting: image security check…. Weekday working hours limit download speed, so a large image's first start can take much longer. docker pull checks that the image exists and prints its digest; the container fetches it when it starts.

docs.title: Private Docker Hub images
docs.text:
1. Run docker login and sign in with a Docker Hub access token (read-only scope is enough) in place of your password. It takes -u, -p and --password-stdin, or asks for them. It prints Login Succeeded.
  2. Use the image: docker pull, docker run, or FROM in a docker build Dockerfile. docker info shows the signed-in Docker Hub user.
  3. Run docker logout to remove the login.

The login is personal. It works in every project and workspace you use, and other members can't use it. The platform keeps the token in its registry, never in your storage. Only Docker Hub (docker.io) is supported. Project managers and administrators can open a shell in your workspace, so they can act with your login there; use a read-only token. If your account shares a workspace name with another account, docker login is refused; ask an administrator.

For a private image, the platform tries your login first, then the project's Docker Hub account (see Projects). A container that is already running keeps running after docker logout, but a restart fails to pull the image.

A build with a private FROM image is stored in your project like any build, so every project member can run it, including the private base layers.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Limit Value Size 1 CPU and 4 GiB per container by default Project quota Container CPU, memory and GPU count toward your project's quota, and GPUs also toward GPU hours. A container that shares the workspace's GPU adds none. Containers per workspace 50 running or waiting. --keep containers have their own limit of 50 per project member. Beyond it, docker run fails with too many containers. Running at once Twice your project's per-user job limit for you in one project (20 when the project sets none), counting your workspace and its containers. Finished containers that aren't removed yet count toward a total of 60. Job limits A container that runs with its workspace doesn't count toward your project's concurrent job limit. A --keep container does. Finished containers Listed in docker ps -a, with their logs, for 24 hours after they finish. --rm, docker rm and docker container prune remove them sooner. Environment values -e values go straight to the container. Other project members can't see them.

Pausing

When the platform pauses a workspace to free its GPU (see Paused instead of stopped on Concepts & Roles), it stops the workspace's containers first. They don't come back on resume.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command What it does docker run Starts a container. Takes -d -i -t -e --env-file -v --mount -w -u --cpus -m --gpus --name --rm --keep --entrypoint -p --shm-size. --pull and --platform are accepted and only print a note. docker exec, attach, cp Run a command in, join, or copy files to and from a running container docker ps [-a] [-q] [--format] [-f] List your containers in this project, from all your workspaces. -a adds the ones that finished in the last 24 hours. docker logs [-f] [--tail N] [-t] [--since] Show a container's output docker stop [-t N], kill [-s SIGNAL], rm [-f] Stop (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10 seconds), send a signal, or remove containers docker wait, inspect, port Print exit codes, details or published ports docker build, images, pull Build an image, list your project's builds, check that an image exists. A missing or private image fails with pull access denied (exit 1). docker login [-u] [-p] [--password-stdin], logout Sign in to or out of Docker Hub. See Private Docker Hub images. docker container ls, rm, prune, docker system prune The long forms. prune removes finished containers only. docker info, version Show your project, queue and GPUs

Unsupported; each prints what to do instead:

Not supported Why compose, network, volume There is no multi-container runtime, no user-defined network and no named volume. Start each service with docker run -d, and mount folders from your storage. push, commit, save, load, tag, rmi Images stay in your project. Use docker build -t NAME:TAG. start, restart, pause, unpause A finished container can't start again. Run a new one. stats, top, events The platform doesn't collect them. Use docker exec NAME top, or docker ps and docker wait. -P, --network, --privileged, --cap-add, --device, --restart, --ipc, --pid, UDP ports, exec -u Containers share the platform's network, run isolated, never run privileged, and can't add Linux capabilities.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: What you see What it means Waiting: image security check… stays on screen The container hasn't started. A new image waits for its security check, and a busy queue waits for resources. Leave the command open, or run with -d and follow it with docker logs -f. Exit code 125 The container never started: the image couldn't be fetched (for example pull access denied), was blocked by the security check (the reason says blocked by the platform), or an option was invalid. The reason prints above the exit, and the container is removed for you. Exit code 126 or 127 The command in the image isn't executable (126) or doesn't exist (127). Check the image's ENTRYPOINT and your command. Exit code 143 docker stop, docker kill or Ctrl-C ended the container with SIGTERM. Exit code 137 The container was killed. It ran out of memory (docker inspect NAME shows "OOMKilled": true, so raise -m), it ignored SIGTERM for 10 seconds, or its workspace stopped. Permission denied or Operation not permitted right after start, for an image such as nginx The image's main process needs root, and the image declares no numeric USER, so the container runs as user 1000. Add -u 0 in a project that allows root containers, or use an unprivileged variant of the image, for example nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged. port is already allocated A program or another container already uses that port of the workspace. Pick another host port, and check docker ps. Conflict. The container name "/web" is already in use A container with that name still exists, even if it finished in the last 24 hours. Run docker rm web, or choose another name. Invalid container name Use 2 to 63 letters, digits, _, . and -, starting and ending with a letter or digit. can not get logs from container which is dead or marked for removal The container's logs are gone: its workspace stopped, or it was removed. this workspace has no GPU to share The workspace has no GPU. Use --keep --gpus N, or start a workspace with a GPU. is outside your workspace storage or named volumes are not supported Mount a folder under your home or a group storage folder. invalid or expired workspace token Retry once. If it persists, delete the workspace and start a new one. restart your workspace for full docker support The workspace is older than the update. Delete it and start a new one. docker pull prints only a reminder there, and docker login asks for a restart. pull access denied for X, repository does not exist or may require 'docker login' The image doesn't exist, or it is private and neither your login nor the project account can read it. Run docker login. the IDE is already signed in to the platform registry; to sign the CLI in, run cscc-cli login after docker login The workspace started from an older image. Restart it; it then starts from the current image. docker login fails with too many Docker Hub login attempts, try again in a minute Too many attempts. Wait a minute and retry.

docs.title: Token Management
docs.text:
List your active API tokens:

cscc-cli tokens list

Revoke a token by ID:

cscc-cli tokens revoke <token-id>

Sign out on this machine:

cscc-cli logout

Logging out revokes the current token and removes it from the config file; hand-added certificate settings stay.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
Setting Default Notes Token lifetime 90 days Make a new token when the old one expires Active tokens per user 20 Revoke unused tokens if you hit the limit Failed sign-ins before lockout 5 Applies to both the dashboard and the CLI Lockout duration 15 min Wait, or ask an admin to unlock your account

Admins can change these values.

docs.title: How things fit together
docs.text:
A group holds projects. A project runs workspaces and uses storage.

Item What it is Group A team or lab. It has shared storage and can be a member of projects. Project Where your resources live. It holds the GPU/CPU quotas, config files, and deployments. Workspace JupyterLab or VS Code in your browser. It uses the project's quota. Storage volume Disk space that keeps your files after a workspace restarts.

docs.title: Quota and resource plans
docs.text:
An admin gives each project a Resource Plan. Starting a workspace checks the project quota and your own quota. The plan also sets:

  • Allowed GPU models. The launch form only shows these.
  • A Schedule Window (when you can start work) and optional Burst Windows (when priority queues are open). See Plan Window below.
  • One or more queues you can pick, each with its own priority, preemption and GPU model rules.

docs.title: Scheduling queues, priority, and preemption
docs.text:
Every workload picks a scheduling queue. A queue has a priority, may be preemptible, and may have a deserved GPU number:

Concept Meaning Priority When GPUs are scarce, higher-priority queues go first. Preemptible Work in this queue can be stopped to free GPUs for higher-priority queues. Deserved GPU The number of GPUs the queue keeps even when other queues compete. 0 means none is guaranteed, so this queue is the first to give GPUs up.

The workspace and deploy forms list the queues your plan allows. The default queue also needs an active plan that allows it.

docs.title: Paused instead of stopped
docs.text:
When a preemptible workload uses one GPU and runs as a single process, the platform pauses it instead of stopping it: its memory and GPU state are saved, the GPU goes to the higher-priority job, and the workload continues from the same point on the same node once that GPU is free again. You get a bell notification when it pauses and again when it resumes. A pause can wait up to 7 days; after that the workload is stopped and reported as preempted.

Limits:

  • Only single-GPU, single-process workloads are paused. Multi-GPU jobs, jobs that share GPU memory between processes, and jobs using CUDA unified memory are stopped as before.
  • Open network connections are closed at the pause. Reopen the notebook or SSH session after the resume; a training script that streams to an external service must reconnect on its own.
  • Work done in the last few minutes before the pause may be repeated after the resume. Writes to databases or object storage in that window can happen twice.
  • Untick Allow pausing when preempted in the deploy or workspace form for a workload that must never be paused; it is then stopped instead. The label platform-go/checkpoint: "false" in a deploy YAML does the same.
  • While paused, a job shows Paused with the pause time at the top of Pods in the project's Resources tab, and in Workspaces; the row returns to Running on its own. A paused workspace cannot be opened or started again until it resumes. Delete ends it for good, and you can then start a new one.

docs.title: Plan window
docs.text:
A plan has two weekly time settings, both in Taiwan time (UTC+8).

Schedule Window is when you can start work. Outside it you cannot submit anything new, even on a priority queue. The default queue follows the same rule. Work that is already running follows the plan's stop policy.

Burst Windows open extra priority queues, but only while the Schedule Window is also open. If Burst Windows is empty, there are no priority hours.

When a burst window closes:

  • Work that already finished is not affected.
  • About 5–6 minutes later, work still running on a priority queue is not restarted. It moves to the plan's normal queue for the same GPU model and gets that queue's priority. It can only be preempted if that queue is Preemptible. You get a bell notification.
  • If the plan has no normal queue for that GPU model, the work is stopped instead, and you get a separate notification.

Example: the schedule is 09:00–18:00 and the burst is 13:00–15:00. Ordinary queues work from 09:00 to 18:00, and priority queues from 13:00 to 15:00. The dashboard counts down each one separately.

Priority is not a reservation

A priority queue puts you at the front of the line. It does not stop long jobs that are already running, so on a full cluster you may still wait for a card.

docs.title: GPU claims
docs.text:
You get a GPU through a claim. A claim says:

  • GPU model: which GPU.
  • SM share: how much of that GPU's compute you get, as a percentage.
  • VRAM policy: elastic shares GPU memory with other workloads. hard cap sets a strict limit.

There are two kinds:

  • Inline claim: made for you when you start a workspace. It goes away with that workspace.
  • Project GPU claim: you create it on a project's GPU Claims tab and reuse it across deployments. It takes GPU quota the moment you create it, but it only counts GPU-hours while a workload is using it.

A project config file points to a project GPU claim through a claim slot (for example train-a). The slot name is only a label; the deploy dialog asks which claim fills it. All replicas of a Deployment share one claim and count once. If only some replicas need a GPU, split them into separate Deployments.

docs.title: GPU-hour budget
docs.text:
A resource plan can also cap the total GPU time a project uses. One GPU-hour is one GPU running for one hour; part of a GPU counts as that part of an hour.

An admin sets how often the budget resets for each project: monthly by default, or weekly, or every set number of hours. Your project's Overview tab shows how much you have used and when it resets. When the budget runs out, new GPU jobs and workspaces are blocked until the reset. Jobs already running keep going.

docs.title: System Roles
docs.text: Permission User Manager Admin Use workspaces within quota ✓ ✓ ✓ Create personal projects ✓ ✓ ✓ Submit resource requests ✓ ✓ ✓ Access admin panel ✓ ✓ Manage all users / groups ✓ Define resource plans ✓ Manage platform queues ✓ View audit logs ✓ ✓ Manage roles and permissions ✓

docs.title: Project Roles
docs.text: Permission Member Manager Admin Launch workspaces ✓ ✓ ✓ View project configs ✓ ✓ ✓ Edit config files ✓ ✓ Manage deployments ✓ ✓ Add/remove members ✓

docs.title: Group Roles
docs.text: Permission User Manager Admin Access group storage ✓ ✓ ✓ View group members ✓ ✓ ✓ Set storage permissions ✓ ✓ Add/remove members ✓

docs.title: Storage permissions
docs.text:
• Group storage permissions come from the group. Group members always get them, and a project cannot change that.
  • The project's Storage page shows those permissions but you cannot edit them there.
  • To change a group member's access, use the group page. For project members who are not in the group, use the project page. People outside the project cannot be given storage access from the project.

docs.title: Key terms
docs.text: Term Definition Storage volume Disk space that keeps your files after a workspace restarts Scheduling Queue A named set of rules for priority, preemption, queue windows, and which GPU models it can use Plan Window Your weekly hours (UTC+8). Burst Windows add priority queues within those hours Preemption Stopping work in a preemptible queue so higher-priority work can run GPU Claim Your hold on a GPU. A project claim takes quota when you create it and counts GPU-hours only while a workload uses it GPU-hour One GPU running for one hour. A plan's GPU-hour budget is the most a project can use before the budget resets (monthly by default) Config File A deployment definition. Every save makes a new version, and old versions never change SM share The percentage of a GPU's compute you get Resource Plan A template that sets a project's GPU, CPU and memory limits, allowed GPU models, and schedule window Workspace JupyterLab or VS Code in your browser

docs.title: GPU desktops
docs.text:
A GPU desktop is a Linux desktop for GUI tools, or a streamed Isaac Sim session, that runs on a platform GPU and opens in your browser.

Who can use it: members of a project where an admin has turned on Remote Desktop Permission. If none of your projects has it, the page says Remote Desktop is not enabled for any of your projects. Ask an admin.

docs.title: Where to find it
docs.text: Sidebar → Workspace → GPU Desktops lists every desktop in your projects. You can't create one there; start it from a project config file (see Start a desktop).

docs.title: Start a desktop
docs.text:
You need the Manager role in the project.

  1. Open Projects → [your project] → Config and click New File.
  2. In the Resource Wizard, add a Pod (or Deployment with one replica) with one container and its image, CPU, and memory.
  3. Turn on the Remote desktop switch under the container. Your image is not rebuilt.
  4. Fill in the desktop fields:
Field What to choose Desktop type Linux desktop (your image, shown inside a desktop) or Isaac Sim WebRTC (the platform's Isaac Sim image, streamed) GPU device class The GPU model GPU reservation 25% GPU, 50% GPU, 75% GPU, or 100% GPU. Below 100% you share the card with others. 100% is all yours Bitrate profile Economy (1600×900, 30 fps), Default (1920×1080, 30 fps), or High motion (1920×1080, 60 fps). Pick Economy when you are off campus
  1. Click Save, then Deploy the version and pick a queue; the plan window applies.
  2. In GPU Desktops, click Connect when the row says Ready.

Rules for a remote-desktop workload

  • Use one container, one replica, and no GPU request or GPU claim of your own. The desktop fields above cover the GPU.
  • Isaac Sim WebRTC needs the platform's Isaac Sim image and the VPN. Mount one storage volume, read-write, at /workspace, and nothing else. Set CPU and memory yourself, within the project quota. One session used about 10 cores and 19 GB.
  • Only storage volumes (personal or group) can be mounted. Other volume types are rejected.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
Status What it means What you can do Pending Waiting for a GPU and encoder slot Wait Starting Getting ready Wait Ready Running, ready to connect Connect Degraded Running, with a warning in the row (for example software encoding: slower and heavier on CPU) Connect still works Failed Could not start Delete, then deploy again Stopping Shutting down Wait Expired Its time ran out Delete, then deploy again when you need it

A row shows status, name, project, GPU model, encoder, image and expiry time, plus the reason when it is not Ready (red for Failed, amber otherwise). An image with no graphics libraries can't open, and its row has no Connect. Failed and Expired rows have Delete.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
• Linux desktop: Connect opens the desktop in a new browser window.
  • Isaac Sim WebRTC: Connect opens the viewer at GPU Desktops → [desktop]. Click the stream to control it with your keyboard and mouse. Leave control gives them back to the browser, and Full screen fills the screen. Quality switches between 1080p and 720p; pick 720p when the picture stutters on Wi-Fi or off campus. Changing it reconnects the stream. Stay on the VPN; if the viewer says VPN media authorization expired, reconnect the VPN and reload the page. If it says The video stream did not start or The stream stopped, click Retry; if that keeps failing, delete the desktop and create a new one.

The open viewer renews its connection every 2 minutes. Closing the tab doesn't stop the desktop.

docs.title: Lifetime
docs.text:
• A desktop lasts at most 8 hours, or less if the project's Max workspace continuous runtime (Settings tab) or the queue's runtime limit is shorter. The row shows the expiry time.
  • A desktop nobody watches for 30 minutes is reclaimed to free the GPU. An open viewer tab counts as watching.
  • When it ends, only files in the mounted storage volume stay. Deploy the config file again for a fresh desktop.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
The GPU Desktops page is empty.

No desktop is running. Deploy a config file with Remote desktop on (see Start a desktop). If the page says Remote Desktop is not enabled, ask an admin.

The status stays Pending.

It is waiting for a free GPU slice or video encoder. A 100% reservation waits for a whole free card.

The row says Degraded. Is it broken?

No. Usually it is software encoding because the machine has no hardware encoder. Connect works, with more lag.

Where are my files?

In the mounted storage volume (for Isaac Sim, /workspace); nothing else survives the desktop.

Can I keep the desktop for more than 8 hours?

No. Deploy again after it ends; the same volume is mounted.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: Who can use it: anyone with a platform account. Read the acceptable use rules first.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Requirement Details Browser Chrome, Firefox, Edge, or Safari (latest version) Account Username and password from your platform admin VPN app An OpenVPN-compatible app (Step 1)

VPN is required

Connect to the VPN first, or the dashboard will not open.

docs.title: Step 1 — Install a VPN app
docs.text: OS Recommended app Install Windows OpenVPN Connect Download installer from the official site macOS Tunnelblick or OpenVPN Connect brew install --cask tunnelblick Linux OpenVPN CLI sudo apt install openvpn or sudo dnf install openvpn

docs.title: Step 2 — Connect to the VPN
docs.text:
1. Get the VPN profile (Platform-VPN.ovpn) from your administrator.
  2. Import it into your VPN app:
    • Windows / macOS GUI: drag the .ovpn file onto the client window, or use Import Profile.
    • Linux CLI: sudo openvpn --config Platform-VPN.ovpn
  3. When prompted, enter your platform username and password (the same credentials you use to sign in).
  4. Wait until the app shows a green light or Initialization Sequence Completed.

docs.title: Step 3 — Sign in to the platform
docs.text:
1. Open your browser and go to: 
    https://dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw
  2. Fill in the three fields:
Field Description Username Your platform account username Password Your platform account password CAPTCHA Type the 4-digit number shown in the image
  1. Click SIGN IN.

Figure 1: Login page with username, password, and CAPTCHA fields.

CAPTCHA

Click the image to refresh an unreadable CAPTCHA.

docs.title: Step 4 — Explore the Home Dashboard
docs.text:
You land on the Home Dashboard. Each widget is explained in Home dashboard.

Widget What it shows Platform GPU Available Free vs. allocated GPU units across the platform GPU Cluster Status How much of each GPU is in use right now; machines appear under anonymous labels Project count (header line) How many projects you belong to, and how many of them have a plan Resource Usage History Live quota usage for each project that has a plan Recent Activity Your recent requests My GPU Jobs Your running GPU jobs with GPU share, memory, and running time

Figure 2: Home dashboard showing GPU availability, GPU cluster status, and My GPU Jobs.

docs.title: Step 5 — Check your project
docs.text:
1. Click Projects in the left sidebar (Workspace section).
  2. Find your personal project, named after your username. Every account has one.
  3. Click the project card to see its quota (GPU, CPU, Memory limits) and members.

Figure 3: Projects page showing personal project card with quota summary.

No project visible?

Ask your admin to add you to a project or group, or to check that your account is fully set up.

docs.title: Step 6 — Launch your first workspace
docs.text:
1. Click Workspaces in the left sidebar.
  2. Click New Workspace.
  3. Fill in the launch form:
Field What to choose Project Your project (personal or team) Environment JupyterLab or VS Code Image One of the platform's images: Base Notebook, PyTorch, TensorFlow, CUDA Dev, or a "(Root)" variant CPU Number of CPU cores, for example 2 Memory RAM in GB, for example 8 GPU Number of GPUs Compute quota (%) How much of each GPU you get: 25% is a quarter of a card, 100% is a whole card GPU memory quota (%) How much of the GPU's memory you get; leave Follow compute on and it matches the compute quota Storage Volumes Tick the volumes you want. Personal storage mounts at /home/<your username>, group volumes at /mnt/shared/<volume name>
  1. Click Start.
  2. Wait for the badge to change from Starting (yellow) to Running (green).
  3. Click Open. Your workspace opens in a new browser tab.

Figure 4: Workspace creation form with project, IDE type, and resource fields.

Workspace won't start?

  • Check that your project still has quota left.
  • Ask your admin if the project's plan window is open right now.
  • GPU images take longer the first time you start one.

docs.title: Step 7 — Manage your storage
docs.text:
1. Click Storage in the left sidebar (Resources section). The My Storage tab opens.
  2. Click Start FileBrowser.
  3. Click Open FileBrowser. In the window that opens, upload, download, rename, and organize files.
  4. Files here stay when a workspace stops. Click Stop FileBrowser when you are done.

Figure 5: FileBrowser interface showing personal storage contents.

docs.title: Step 8 — Join a group (optional)
docs.text:
1. Click Groups in the left sidebar.
  2. Look through the groups, or ask your admin to add you.
  3. Group members share a group storage volume, good for datasets and shared models.
  4. Group managers can set each person's access to shared storage (Read / Write / None).

docs.title: Running your own container
docs.text: For a long training job or a service, deploy a container from the project's Config tab instead of a workspace. You need the Manager role in the project, and you already have it in your personal project. See Projects → Config file versioning.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
VPN shows connected but the dashboard does not open

Import the profile again and reconnect. Some VPN apps also need DNS update scripts turned on. Still stuck? Check that your firewall allows UDP port 31194, then ask your admin.

Can I connect to the VPN from more than one device?

Yes, with the same account at the same time. The VPN app asks for your password once a day.

Advanced: checking the VPN connection by hand

Open a terminal and run nslookup dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw. If the name resolves and the dashboard opens, you are connected.

On Windows, if OpenVPN shows connected but 192.168.109.1 is unreachable, open PowerShell and run route print | findstr 192.168.109. The output should include a 192.168.109.0 route through the OpenVPN adapter. If it is missing, re-import the latest Platform-VPN.ovpn. The profile pushes the platform DNS server for cscc.nthu.edu.tw and turns on block-outside-dns, so Windows uses only that DNS server while connected. Resolve-DnsName dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw confirms platform DNS; http://192.168.109.1:30080 is a low-level connectivity check.

CAPTCHA is wrong but I typed it correctly

The code is 4 digits. Click the image for a new one.

Login fails with 'Invalid credentials'

Use your username, not your email address. If your password changed recently, the old one no longer works.
